45033: Adam and Christ: two heads of humanity
45034: The first human, formed from the dust and given life by God's breath. He was placed in the garden to keep it and to obey one command. His disobedience brought death, toil and exile, and his children inherited his likeness.
45035: Jesus is the head of a new humanity. Where Adam's one act of disobedience brought condemnation and death to many, Jesus' one act of obedience brings righteousness and life. Adam became a living being; Christ became a life-giving Spirit.
45037: One man's obedience affects all who belong to him
45038: Tested in a wilderness and in the garden of Gethsemane and holds firm
45040: From heaven; believers will bear his heavenly image
45041: Given all authority, with everything put under his feet
45042: Paul stresses that the two are not equal: 'the free gift is not like the trespass' (Rom 5:15). Adam's act was one sin leading to condemnation; Christ's gift answers many sins and brings justification. Adam was a created man; Christ is the Lord from heaven.
45043: Developed recapitulation: Christ goes back over the whole human story Adam spoiled and gets it right at every point, summing humanity up in himself.
45044: Read Romans 5 as the root of the doctrine of original sin: all humanity was somehow 'in Adam'. This reading shaped the Western church but is debated by Eastern Orthodox theologians, who speak of inherited mortality rather than inherited guilt.
45045: Paul says Adam was a 'pattern' (Greek *typos*) of the one to come. Think of two family trees. Everyone starts in Adam's family, which ends in death. Jesus starts a new family, and those joined to him share his life. This is the clearest example of a type in the whole Bible, because Paul uses the very word.
45046: How exactly humanity is 'in Adam' (guilt, corruption, mortality, or all three) is debated between Western and Eastern traditions, and modern discussion of human origins adds further questions. The typology itself does not settle those debates.
45047: Eve and the bride: the church from Christ's side
45049: God takes a rib from the sleeping Adam and builds the woman. Adam greets her as bone of his bones, and the two become one flesh. She is named the mother of all living.
45051: Christ loves the church, gives himself for her and makes her holy, as a husband with his bride. Paul quotes Genesis 2:24 and says it is a great mystery about Christ and the church.
45053: Christ sleeps in death on the cross
45054: Blood and water flow from Christ's pierced side, read as the sacraments that build the church
45055: The church is Christ's body, united with him
45056: Paul fears the church may be led astray as Eve was
45057: Eve was deceived and shared in the fall; the bride of Revelation is pictured finally pure and ready. Paul never calls Eve a typos; he draws the marriage analogy from Genesis 2:24 rather than from Eve as a person. The 'side' link (John 19:34) is a later reading, not stated in the NT.
45058: Compared Adam's sleep and opened side to Christ's death and pierced side, from which the church, the true mother of the living, was formed.
45059: Repeatedly said the church was formed from the side of the sleeping Christ just as Eve was formed from the side of sleeping Adam.
45060: Paired Eve not only with the church but with Mary: Eve's disobedience was untied by Mary's obedience. This Eve–Mary parallel is a separate, traditional typology.
45061: The Bible begins and ends with a wedding. In Genesis a bride is made from the first man's side; in Revelation the church is presented as the bride of the Lamb. Paul says the marriage of Genesis 2 points to Christ and the church.
45062: The NT links marriage in Genesis to Christ and the church, but the details (the sleep, the side, the rib) are developed by the Fathers. The Eve–Mary parallel is traditional and especially important in Catholic and Orthodox devotion; Protestants generally do not adopt it.
45063: Abel's blood and the blood that speaks better
45065: Abel offers an acceptable sacrifice and is killed by his jealous brother Cain. God says Abel's blood cries out from the ground.
45066: Jesus, the righteous one killed by his brothers
45067: Jesus, the innocent one, is killed through the envy of his own people. His sprinkled blood speaks a better word than Abel's: not a cry for vengeance but a word of forgiveness and covenant.
45068: The good shepherd who is himself the offering
45071: Jesus names Abel's blood at the head of the line his generation will answer for
45072: Hebrews uses Abel by contrast: his blood calls for justice, Christ's blood brings mercy. Abel was a sinner like everyone else and his death achieved nothing for others; Christ's death is described as redemptive.
45073: In his Easter sermon lists Abel among the figures in whom Christ suffered beforehand: murdered in Abel, bound in Isaac, sold in Joseph, exposed in Moses, hunted in David.
45074: Read Cain and Abel as the start of the two cities: Cain founds an earthly city, Abel is a pilgrim, a figure of Christ and his people.
45075: Abel was the first person in the Bible to die, killed by his own brother. His blood 'cried out' for justice. Hebrews says Jesus' blood also speaks, but it says something better: it brings people near to God instead of calling down judgement.
45076: The NT text uses Abel more as a contrast than as a foreshadowing pattern. Calling Abel a 'type' is fair in the Fathers' sense, but the Hebrews link is comparative rather than a stated typos.
45077: Enoch, the man who walked with God and was taken
45078: Enoch walked with God and then 'was not, for God took him'. Hebrews says he was taken so that he should not see death, and Jude cites him as a prophet of judgement.
45079: Christ's ascension and the hope of believers
45080: Later readers saw in Enoch a picture of a righteous person received into God's presence, foreshadowing Christ's ascension and the final transformation of believers who are alive at his return.
45082: The Son lives in perfect communion with the Father
45083: Those alive at Christ's coming are changed without dying
45084: Christ announces and carries out the final judgement
45085: Enoch did not die; Christ did die and then rose before ascending, so the ascension is not a copy of Enoch's translation. The NT never calls Enoch a type of Christ; Hebrews uses him as an example of faith.
45086: Cited Enoch (with Elijah) as evidence that God can preserve a human body in life, supporting bodily resurrection.
45088: Several early writers identified Enoch and Elijah as the two witnesses of Revelation 11, who would return to die. This is tradition, not stated in Scripture.
45089: Enoch is famous for one line: he walked with God, and then God took him. Christians have seen him as a small preview of the hope that death does not have the last word, and that God can bring a person straight into his presence.
45090: This is a traditional, fairly light typology. The book of 1 Enoch, quoted in Jude, is canonical only in the Ethiopian Orthodox church; it should not be used to build NT typology. The Enoch-and-Elijah-as-two-witnesses idea is tradition.
45093: God tells Noah to build an ark. Eight people and the animals are carried safely through the waters of judgement that destroy the old world, and they step out into a washed creation.
45095: Peter says the water that saved Noah's family corresponds to baptism, which now saves, not by washing dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus.
45096: Baptism as dying to the old life
45098: Rising to new life with the risen Christ
45099: The Spirit descends like a dove at Jesus' baptism
45100: The flood killed the wicked; baptism is offered to them. Peter insists the saving power is not the water itself but Christ's resurrection and the pledge of a good conscience. The ark carried the righteous; the church holds sinners being made righteous.
45101: Saw the eight people as pointing to the eighth day, the day of resurrection, and linked the wood of the ark to the wood of the cross.
45102: Compared the dove returning to the ark with the Spirit coming to the baptised.
45103: Read the ark as a figure of the church and even of Christ's body, with the door in its side matching the wound in Christ's side.
45104: Noah's family went through a world-ending flood and came out alive because they were inside the ark. Peter says baptism is like that: you pass through water that signals death to the old life, and you come out safe because you are joined to the risen Jesus.
45105: Peter's word is *antitypon*, so the link is explicit. What baptism actually does is debated (see /debates/baptism): sacramental traditions read 'baptism now saves you' strongly; others stress Peter's qualification that it is the appeal of a good conscience. The patristic idea that there is no salvation outside the ark-church is an application, not part of Peter's text.
45107: A king of Salem and priest of God Most High who brings bread and wine to Abraham, blesses him, and receives a tenth of the spoils. Psalm 110 later speaks of a royal priest 'after the order of Melchizedek'.
45109: Hebrews argues that Jesus is a priest not from Levi's tribe but in Melchizedek's line: a king-priest whose priesthood rests on an indestructible life, so he lives forever to intercede.
45110: Christ is royal Son and high priest
45112: Christ's priesthood does not depend on ancestry and has no end
45113: Christ's priesthood is greater than the Levitical one
45114: Read by many traditions as foreshadowing the Lord's Supper
45115: Hebrews says Melchizedek was 'made like' the Son of God, not that he was the Son; the silence about his parents is an argument from what Genesis leaves out. Melchizedek blessed Abraham once; Christ offered himself once for all and intercedes forever.
45116: Argued that the bread and wine Melchizedek offered prefigured the eucharist, and used it to insist the cup must contain wine.
45117: Used Melchizedek's offering as evidence that the Christian sacraments are older than those of the Jews.
45118: Melchizedek appears for three verses in Genesis and disappears. Hebrews uses the mystery around him to make a point: Jesus is a priest of a different and higher kind than the priests descended from Aaron, because his priesthood rests on his endless life, not on family descent.
45119: Hebrews never mentions the bread and wine, so the eucharistic link is traditional. Some interpreters, ancient and modern, have argued Melchizedek was a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ; most read Hebrews 7:3 as typology from the silence of Genesis. Qumran's 11QMelchizedek shows Jews of the time also speculated about him.
45122: God tests Abraham by asking him to offer Isaac, his beloved and only son of promise. Isaac carries the wood up the mountain; Abraham says God will provide the lamb. At the last moment God stops him and provides a ram.
45124: God did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us. Hebrews says Abraham reasoned God could raise the dead, and received Isaac back 'as a figure' of resurrection.
45126: Jesus carries his cross to Golgotha
45130: Isaac was not sacrificed; a substitute died instead. In the antitype there is no substitute for the Son: he is himself the substitute. Abraham's hand was stopped; the Father's was not.
45131: Treated Isaac as a figure of Christ who was bound, and the ram as the one who was actually slain.
45132: Preached that Isaac carrying the wood is like Christ carrying the cross, and that Isaac as priest and victim both pictures Christ.
45133: Noted that Isaac carried the wood as Christ carried his cross.
45134: Abraham was asked to give up the son he loved most, and then God stopped him. Christians read the story as a rehearsal: what God did not require of Abraham, he did himself in giving Jesus. Paul's wording 'did not spare his own Son' seems to echo God's words to Abraham.
45135: Romans 8:32 echoes the Greek of Genesis 22:16 but does not name Isaac, and Hebrews 11:19 says 'figuratively' (*en parabolē*) about receiving Isaac back, not about the sacrifice as a whole. Jewish tradition developed the Akedah in its own way, sometimes stressing Isaac's willing consent. The identification of Moriah with the later temple mount rests on 2 Chr 3:1; with Golgotha it is tradition.
45136: The ram caught in the thicket
45138: Abraham looks up and sees a ram caught by its horns in a thicket. He offers it in place of his son and names the place 'The LORD will provide'.
45140: Jesus dies in the place of others, the provision God makes so that the guilty go free.
45141: Dies in the place of sinners
45144: The ram was an animal with no will in the matter; Christ gave himself freely. Note that Abraham predicted a lamb and God provided a ram: the 'lamb' language waits for the NT.
45145: Said the Lord was the lamb like the ram that Abraham saw caught in the bush, and that the bush pointed to the cross.
45146: Connected the ram caught by its horns with Christ crowned with thorns.
45147: Isaac did not die because something died in his place. Christians see in the ram the simplest picture of what they believe about the cross: someone else took the death that was due.
45148: No NT text mentions the ram. The thorns-and-thicket link is a devotional observation from the Fathers, not an argument the NT makes. Whether 'substitution' is the main or only meaning of the cross is debated (see /debates/atonement).
45150: Joseph is his father's beloved son, hated and sold by his brothers, falsely accused and imprisoned. He is then raised to the right hand of Pharaoh and saves many lives, including the brothers who betrayed him.
45152: Jesus is rejected by his own, sold for silver, condemned though innocent, and then exalted to God's right hand, from where he offers forgiveness and life to those who rejected him.
45154: Sold by a disciple for thirty pieces of silver
45155: Falsely accused and crucified between criminals
45156: Raised to the right hand of God
45157: Human wickedness and God's plan meet in the cross
45158: His own did not receive him (John 1:11)
45159: Joseph had faults (his early boasting) and sometimes tested his brothers harshly. His saving work was about famine and food, not sin and death. He was not killed.
45160: Lists Joseph as one in whom the Lord was sold beforehand.
45161: Wrote a whole treatise on Joseph as a model of chastity and a figure of Christ.
45162: Joseph's story has the shape of the gospel: the favoured son is rejected by his brothers, goes down into the pit and prison, is raised to power, and uses it to save the very people who wronged him. The NT never says 'Joseph was a type', but Stephen tells his story as part of a pattern of Israel rejecting the deliverers God sent.
45163: This is one of the most popular types but has no explicit NT warrant. Stephen's speech (Acts 7) makes the 'rejected deliverer' pattern visible with Joseph and Moses, but it does not draw the line to Jesus in so many words. Popular preaching sometimes stretches it to every detail (the coat, the cup, Asenath as the gentile church).
45164: Moses and the prophet like Moses
45165: Moses is saved as a baby from a king's massacre, called to lead Israel out of slavery, speaks with God face to face, gives the law and mediates the covenant. He promised that God would raise up a prophet like him.
45167: Peter and Stephen identify Jesus as the promised prophet like Moses. Hebrews says Moses was faithful as a servant in God's house; Christ is faithful as the Son over it.
45168: Escapes as an infant when Herod kills Bethlehem's boys
45169: Teaches with authority on a mountain (Matt 5-7)
45174: Moses was a sinner who was barred from the land; Jesus is presented as sinless. Moses brought a law that, as John says, came through him, while grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. Moses was a servant in the house; Jesus is the Son over it.
45175: Includes Moses exposed on the river among the figures of Christ's sufferings.
45176: Wrote the *Life of Moses*, reading his whole career as a picture of the soul's ascent to God, with many Christ-figures along the way.
45177: Moses promised that one day God would send another prophet like him, and the Jews of Jesus' day were still waiting for that figure. The apostles say Jesus is that prophet. Matthew especially tells Jesus' early life so that it echoes Moses' story.
45178: In its original setting Deuteronomy 18 can be read as a promise of a continuing line of prophets; the NT reads it as fulfilled supremely in one prophet. Matthew's Moses-parallels are widely recognised but not all are stated; some (five discourses matching five books) are scholarly proposals.
45179: Aaron and the great high priest
45181: Aaron is anointed as Israel's first high priest. He wears the names of the tribes on his shoulders and breastplate, offers sacrifices, and once a year enters the Most Holy Place with blood to make atonement.
45183: Jesus is the high priest who sympathises with our weakness yet is without sin. He offered himself once for all, entered heaven itself, and always lives to intercede.
45184: Christ did not exalt himself but was appointed
45185: Represents his people before the Father
45188: Has no sins of his own to offer for
45189: Hebrews is mostly about contrast: Aaron's priests died and were replaced, needed to sacrifice for themselves, served in a copy of the heavenly sanctuary, and repeated sacrifices that could not cleanse the conscience. Christ is said to be different on every count. Hebrews also places Jesus in Melchizedek's order, not Aaron's.
45190: Preached on Leviticus 16, reading the high priest entering the sanctuary as Christ entering heaven with his own blood.
45191: Used the ordered Levitical priesthood as a model for order in the church's ministry.
45192: Israel's high priest stood between God and the people. Hebrews says Jesus does that job perfectly and permanently. Where Aaron went into a tent once a year with animal blood, Jesus went into God's presence once for all with his own.
45193: Whether Christian ministers are 'priests' in a sense continuous with Aaron is debated between Catholic/Orthodox and Protestant traditions. Hebrews itself speaks of Christ's unique priesthood and of all believers offering sacrifices of praise (Heb 13:15).
45195: On the night of the exodus each household kills an unblemished lamb, marks the doorposts with its blood, and eats it. The destroyer passes over the marked houses. Not a bone of the lamb is to be broken.
45197: Paul says Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed. John has Jesus die as the Passover lambs are prepared and notes that none of his bones were broken. The Last Supper is set at Passover.
45198: A lamb without blemish or spot (1 Pet 1:19)
45200: Soldiers do not break Jesus' legs
45201: The Lord's Supper remembers Christ's death
45202: Believers clear out malice and wickedness
45203: The Passover lamb was not originally a sin offering; it was a protective sign and a meal. The NT fuses Passover with other sacrifice ideas. Israel repeated Passover every year; Christ died once.
45204: His Easter homily is a full reading of Exodus 12 as the type and Christ as the reality. He compares the type to an artist's model that is set aside once the real statue is finished.
45205: Noted the lamb was roasted on crossed spits, which he took as a figure of the cross.
45206: On the night Israel left Egypt, the blood of a lamb on the door meant death passed over that house. The first Christians, many of them Jews, saw Jesus' death at Passover and said: he is our lamb. This is why Easter in many languages is still called by the Passover name (Pascha).
45207: Whether the Last Supper was itself a Passover meal (the Synoptics) or held the day before (John's timing) is a long-running historical question. Melito's sermon also contains harsh language against the Jewish people that later fed anti-Judaism and should be read critically.
45208: Crossing the Red Sea and baptism
45210: Trapped between Pharaoh's army and the sea, Israel walks through on dry ground while the waters stand as walls. The pursuing army is drowned, and Israel sings of the LORD's victory.
45211: Paul says Israel was 'baptised into Moses in the cloud and in the sea'. These things happened as examples (*typoi*) for us: believers are baptised into Christ and set free from sin's slavery.
45212: Passing through baptism out of sin's slavery
45215: The song of Moses and of the Lamb (Rev 15:3)
45216: Paul's main point is a warning: all were baptised, yet most died in the wilderness. The type shows that the sign alone does not guarantee faithfulness. Israel's deliverance was national and physical; Christian baptism concerns each person's union with Christ.
45217: Read the crossing as a figure of baptism, with Pharaoh's army as the devil left drowned in the water.
45218: Preached the crossing as the soul passing through baptism and leaving the Egyptians, its vices, behind.
45219: Taught newly baptised Christians that Pharaoh stands for the devil, and that in the font they had escaped him as Israel escaped Egypt.
45220: Israel walked through the sea and came out free on the other side, with the slave-masters gone for good. Paul says this was a kind of baptism. The point he presses is sober: they all got wet, but many did not keep trusting God afterwards, so do not presume.
45221: Paul uses the crossing to warn, not mainly to celebrate. The Fathers' detailed allegories (each Egyptian a particular vice) go well beyond Paul.
45222: Manna and the bread of life
45224: God feeds Israel every morning with bread from heaven. It must be gathered daily, cannot be hoarded, and teaches that people do not live by bread alone but by every word from God's mouth.
45226: After feeding five thousand, Jesus says the true bread from heaven is not Moses' manna but himself. Those who ate manna died; whoever eats this bread will live forever.
45227: The Son who comes down from heaven
45231: Jesus makes the contrast himself: the fathers ate manna and died. Manna fed bodies; Jesus speaks of himself as food for eternal life. Manna stopped when Israel entered the land; Christ's provision does not stop.
45232: Preached that the manna and the Lord's bread are both signs, but that what matters is eating inwardly by faith, not merely outwardly.
45233: Argued that the eucharist is greater than the manna, since manna was a shadow and the eucharist is the body of Christ.
45234: Manna was the daily bread God sent to keep Israel alive in the desert. Jesus says he is the real bread from heaven: not food that keeps you going one more day, but life that lasts forever.
45235: How far John 6 refers to the Lord's Supper is debated: Catholic and Orthodox readers see a strong eucharistic meaning; many Protestants read 'eating' mainly as believing (John 6:35). See /debates/lords-supper.
45238: At Rephidim Moses strikes a rock and water flows for the thirsty people. Later at Kadesh he is told to speak to the rock but strikes it twice, and is barred from the land.
45240: Paul says Israel drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, 'and the rock was Christ'. Jesus invites the thirsty to come and drink, and living water flows.
45241: Struck in death; from his side flow blood and water
45242: Living water offered to the undeserving
45243: Christ present with his people throughout their journey
45244: Paul's statement is unusual: he does not only say the rock pictured Christ but that Christ was present with Israel. The rock gave physical water; Christ gives the Spirit. Moses' second striking was an act of disobedience, so it cannot simply be read as 'Christ struck again'.
